title: Fewer international students, billions at stake
source: Axios — Fewer international students, billions at stake (2026-11-16)
body: Fewer international students are enrolling at American universities, costing the American economy billions of dollars and hurting college towns. Why it matters: International students typically pay higher tuition than their American counterparts, helping offset financial challenges and support domestic students. Their absence could hit smaller colleges especially hard, with ripple effects for local economies and the workforce. Driving the news: New international student enrollment at U.S. colleges and universities fell 18% during the 2025–26 academic year, according to data released Monday by the Institute of International Education. Overall international enrollment dropped 3% to about 1.15 million students. International graduate student numbers fell 13%, compared to a 0.3% dip among undergraduates. However, doctoral enrollment rose 3%. Threat level: "For domestic enrollment, we're hitting the demographic cliff," Sarah Spreitzer, vice president and chief of staff for government relations at the American Council on Education, tells Axios. She pointed to fewer high school graduates and state budget cuts as extra financial pressures facing universities. "I think international students were used as one of the levers that you could pull to help address some of the budgetary issues." Domestic students could receive "less support," she said, although it's too soon to know whether that could mean higher tuition or fewer scholarships. By the numbers: International students contributed roughly $40 billion to the U.S. economy in 2025-2026, and those aren't just tuition dollars. Their spending on housing, food and transportation helped support over 300,000 jobs, per data released by NAFSA: Association of International Educators. That's down 7%, or $3 billion, compared to the 2024-2025 academic year, with 46,000 fewer jobs supported. It marks the second straight annual decline after three years of growth. Real estate developers in Boston told Spreitzer last year that declining international enrollment left apartments vacant and affected plans to build more student housing. Between the lines: Spreitzer attributes some of the declining enrollment to the Trump administration's immigration policies. International students "are trading horror stories about being stopped at the border," she says, adding that fears of being denied re-entry is too big of a risk. Eighty-eight percent of institutions reporting declining enrollment cited the visa application process, while 70% cited travel restrictions, per a separate IIE report . Zoom in: Smaller institutions, particularly in the Midwest and away from the coasts, may be experiencing much sharper declines than prestigious universities with stronger international name recognition. Spreitzer contrasted the potential experiences of elite institutions like Harvard with smaller liberal arts colleges that have relatively few international students. A school like Harvard has a massive endowment to help cushion the blow, but others are going to have to make sacrifices. Case in point: At the University of North Texas, the university is phasing out dozens of minors, cutting four master's programs and merging multiple departments to address a projected $45 million deficit. The university has among the highest numbers of international students in Texas, but the declining enrollment is substantially lowering revenue. The bottom line: Universities aren't just losing students for one semester. They're potentially losing years of enrollment, tuition revenue and future research talent. "If that student doesn't come this year, that means we've lost out on many years of their enrollment," Spreitzer says. "So this is going to have a cascading effect."
